project.title: Cada dos días
project.logline: A confusing note becomes a gentle lesson in asking a professional interpreter to clarify the difference between amount and timing.

storyContract.timing: Guide only; recut to the supplied song after listening.
storyContract.safety: Do not show or invent a dose, regimen, medical instruction, legible prescription, pills being taken, or a clinical answer. The misunderstanding concerns words; the answer comes from the healthcare team through a professional interpreter.
storyContract.text: Add exact Spanish copy in post, not in generated images; no generated text or numerical instruction.

lookBlock: Vertical 9:16, tasteful 1990s Spanish-language music video, warmly human and elegant rather than parody: soft 35mm film grain, creamy highlights, honeyed morning sunlight, terracotta, sage green, deep walnut and muted teal, practical tungsten, polished natural wood and understated brass. Realistic adult people with consistent faces and clothes; observational, lyrical camera, gentle rhythmic movement, warm humor only at a verbal misunderstanding. No text, logos, readable notes or medical prescriptions in the generated frames. Compose for portrait and leave lower-safe space for accurate Spanish typography added in post.

characters.Rafa: Rafa, an adult Latino man in his early fifties, salt-and-pepper hair, soft brown eyes, a neat moustache, cream knit polo and brown trousers; affectionate, thoughtful, a little puzzled but never foolish.
characters.Teresa: Teresa, an adult Latina woman in her late forties, dark shoulder-length hair, sage-green blouse and simple gold earrings; warm, observant and gently reassuring, her humor affectionate and restrained.
characters.Interpreter: A professional adult Latina interpreter in her forties, dark hair neatly tied back, midnight-blue tailored jacket over an ivory blouse; calm, attentive, visually distinct from Teresa and accurately conveys the conversation.
characters.Clinician: An adult health-care professional in their fifties with short dark hair, muted teal scrubs under a light jacket; attentive and respectful, speaking with the interpreter at eye level, no invented medical information.

documents.brief:
# Brief

A roughly one-minute vertical Spanish-language music video, Cada dos días, in an elegant, old-time 1990s style. Rafa and Teresa meet a verbal ambiguity with curiosity rather than blame, then a professional interpreter helps a health-care team clarify it. The instruction itself is never shown or invented. The song has been recovered from the user’s Muse project; cut timings remain provisional until checked against its beats and lyrics.
documents.script:
# Script and provisional timing

00–08 La nota: Rafa finds a note, looks at a calendar, and Teresa enters with two cups. Add «Una palabra puede cambiarlo todo». No legible instructions.

08–18 La confusión: Rafa points to consecutive calendar squares; Teresa tilts her head. Transform squares into two question marks in post. Optional Rafa: «¿Dos cada día… o cada dos días?» only over a musical pause.

18–30 Pausa: Teresa raises a hand; freeze briefly. Add separate cards «¿Cuánto?» and «¿Cuándo?» and «No adivines. Pregunta.» Neither card shows a dose.

30–43 Aclarar: a professional interpreter listens to Rafa, asks the health-care team to clarify, listens to their reply, and conveys it. Optional interpreter: «¿Puede confirmar la cantidad y la frecuencia?» The answer is not shown or invented.

43–55 El sentido llega: Rafa nods, relieved. At home Teresa places separate «cantidad» and «frecuencia» cards; they exchange a look and cups gently clink on the beat.

55–60 Cierre: clean background, two speech bubbles joined by a line and «Escuchar. Aclarar. Interpretar.»
documents.look-bible:
# Visual world

A graceful 1990s Spanish-language music video remembered through soft film grain and a honeyed palette. Frame vertically, with intentional close-ups, consistent eyelines and open space for captions. Kitchen is sunny, warm wood and cream ceramic; the fictional consultation is calm teal and ivory. Make the warmth feel lived-in, not sepia nostalgia or comedy at a patient’s expense.
documents.characters:
# People

Rafa and Teresa are adults whose relationship reads through small gestures and a shared kitchen ritual. Rafa is puzzled by language, not portrayed as incompetent. Teresa gives him time. The trained interpreter is a separate professional who listens and conveys the health-care team’s clarification. The clinician listens respectfully. Keep each face and clothing consistent between takes.
documents.lore-bible:
# Continuity and boundaries

Rafa wears cream and Teresa sage in the same warm kitchen. Both cups are cream ceramic. The calendar has blank, unnumbered squares and the note is deliberately illegible. The consultation is fictional. The interpreter and clinician are distinct people. No pill-taking, medical dosage, prescription, instruction or fabricated answer appears on screen or in dialogue. All legible words are added locally.
documents.treatment:
# Treatment

In a sunlit kitchen Rafa turns an unreadable note toward the light and then looks at a calendar. Teresa arrives with two cups. His hesitant fingers mark two neighboring blank squares; her tiny head tilt makes the ambiguity human, not a joke about taking medicine. On-screen Spanish text is placed in post.

Teresa gently raises her hand. A brief freeze gives two questions room to stand apart: ¿Cuánto? and ¿Cuándo? The picture resumes in a fictional consultation, where a professional interpreter listens to Rafa, asks the health-care team to clarify, receives their reply, and relays it. We never see or invent the answer.

Rafa relaxes. At home Teresa sets down the separate ideas cantidad and frecuencia, and the couple share a knowing look. Their cups touch on a real musical accent once the actual track is available. A spare connected-speech-bubble closing card leaves the message: Escuchar. Aclarar. Interpretar.

departments.direction: Play the ambiguity honestly and lightly. Rafa is thinking, Teresa pauses without scolding, and the professional interpreter listens before helping to clarify. The consultation is a respectful exchange, not a demonstration of medicine or an authoritative dose. Leave space for the music and legible post-produced captions.
departments.camera-lighting: Use portrait 9:16 composition and coherent screen direction, with warm diffused sunlight through a kitchen window and soft fill. The consultation uses gentle teal-ivory practical light. Establish the room before restrained close-ups, compose eyes in the upper third, and leave safe space for captions and interface cropping.
departments.production-design: Kitchen: cream cups, unmarked paper, a calendar with anonymous unnumbered squares, honey wood and a sunlit window. No visible pharmacy labels, dose numbers or instructions. Consultation: restrained desk, plain unmarked folders, muted neutral backgrounds, three separate people. Text cards and motion graphics will be authored digitally.
departments.costume-makeup: Rafa keeps his cream knit polo and brown trousers; Teresa wears the same sage blouse and gold earrings in kitchen scenes. Interpreter wears a navy jacket and ivory shirt, clinician muted teal scrubs. Natural 1990s styling, not a celebrity likeness. Keep hands and clothing consistent from cut to cut.
departments.choreography: Each shot contains one legible action and a held end pose. Rafa glances at paper, then calendar; Teresa enters with two cups; fingers point to two adjacent blank squares; she raises a gentle hand. In consultation, listen, ask, listen, convey in separate shots. At home the cards remain distinct and the cups meet gently.
departments.sound-music: The user-provided Cada dos días song has been recovered from the Muse source package and used in the local workprint. The cut follows the script guide and has not yet been checked against the song’s beats and lyrics. Optional dialogue must be recorded separately and used only over a pause; never fabricate an answer. No claim of synchronized singing or finalized mix.
departments.editorial: Draft timing maps to 60 seconds at 24 fps, with source takes of about ten seconds and cuts of 2–4 seconds. Generate video without text; add exact Spanish text and the two-question-mark treatment in post. Preserve clear distinctions between cantidad and frecuencia. Replace provisional cuts after hearing the song, and review the final vertical frame and mix.
